title: What a good contract says, and what it should leave out
author: eleanor-harrow
summary: A short checklist for reading any business agreement before you sign it.
body:
A contract is a plan for what happens when things go differently than expected. If everything goes well, no one looks at it again. The pages that matter are the ones that describe a problem.

## Check the basics first

Confirm that the parties are named correctly, that the work or goods are described in terms you would recognize, and that the price and payment dates are written down. Vague words like "reasonable" and "promptly" invite disagreement. Where you can, replace them with a number of days or an amount.

## Read the exit

Look for how the agreement ends, who can end it and what notice is required. Many disputes are really arguments about whether someone was allowed to stop.

## Leave out what you will not use

Long forms often carry clauses that do not fit your situation. Ask what each one is for. If no one can say, it is worth discussing before you sign.

title: Choosing a structure for a small business in Ohio
author: daniel-vance
summary: Sole proprietorship, partnership or limited liability company: the questions to ask before you file.
body:
Many owners begin as sole proprietors without deciding to. The law treats the owner and the business as the same person, which is simple but leaves personal property exposed to business debts.

## Why owners form a company

A limited liability company separates the two, in most circumstances. It also gives you a place to write down how decisions are made and how an owner can leave. That second point is often more valuable than the first.

## Questions to ask

How many owners will there be? Will anyone put in money but not work in the business? Who signs for loans? What happens if an owner dies or wants out? Answering these before you file saves expensive conversations later.

A short meeting is usually enough to choose a structure and prepare the paperwork.

title: Five signs your employee handbook needs an update
author: naomi-okafor
summary: Handbooks go stale quickly. These are the common signs that yours has.
body:
A handbook is often written once and filed away. Meanwhile the business hires remote staff, changes its hours and adds benefits.

## Signs it is time

The handbook describes procedures no one follows. It mentions job titles that no longer exist. It has no policy on remote work, or on time worked outside normal hours. It was last reviewed before you reached a new employee count. Managers give different answers to the same question.

## What to do

Start by listing how things really work, then compare that with the written policy. Where they differ, decide which one should change. A handbook that matches practice is easier to follow, and easier to defend if a question arises.

title: Reading a commercial lease: six clauses to slow down on
author: marcus-avery
summary: Rent is only part of the cost of a space. These clauses decide the rest.
body:
Tenants usually negotiate the monthly rent and then sign what is put in front of them. Several other clauses affect cost and flexibility just as much.

## Six to read slowly

The term and renewal options. Who pays for taxes, insurance and common area maintenance, and how the shares are calculated. How rent increases. What happens if you want to leave early or assign the lease. Who is responsible for repairs and for returning the space at the end. Whether a personal guarantee is required.

## For landlords

The same clauses protect you when they are written clearly. A lease that both sides understand is the one least likely to be argued about later.

title: Probate in Ohio: the dates that matter
author: elena-moreno
summary: A plain guide to the first months after a loved one has died.
body:
When someone dies, the family is asked to do many things at once. A few have dates attached.

## The first weeks

Locate the will and keep it safe. Order several copies of the death certificate. Notify the bank, the employer and any pension or insurance provider. Do not distribute belongings or pay large bills before speaking with the person who will act as executor.

## Opening the estate

The will is filed with the local probate court, and the executor is appointed. Creditors are notified and have a period to make claims. Only after that period can property be distributed.

Every estate differs, and some are simple enough to handle quickly. A first conversation will tell you which kind you have.

title: Why your will should be reviewed every few years
author: eleanor-harrow
summary: Life changes faster than documents do. A brief review keeps your plan in step.
body:
A will written when children were small may not suit a family with adult children, a new home or a business.

## Moments for a review

A marriage or divorce. A birth or adoption. A death in the family, including a person you named to act for you. A move to another state. The sale or purchase of a business or property. A significant change in what you own.

## What a review involves

We read your documents together, ask what has changed and tell you whether anything needs to be updated. Often the answer is that nothing does, and you leave knowing your plan still works.

title: Parenting plans that last longer than a school year
author: naomi-okafor
summary: Specific schedules and clear decision rules make plans easier to follow.
body:
A parenting plan is a document the whole family lives by. The plans that hold up are specific.

## What to write down

Regular weekly schedules, holidays and school breaks. How and when exchanges happen. How major decisions about school, health and activities are made. How the plan changes as children grow.

## Keep it workable

A schedule that looks fair on paper but does not fit work hours will not last. Think about what a normal week will actually look like, and include a way to revisit the plan so that small problems do not become disputes.

title: Mediation or court: choosing how to resolve a dispute
author: daniel-vance
summary: How to decide when a negotiated settlement is the better route.
body:
Not every dispute should be settled, and not every dispute should be tried. The choice depends on what you need.

## When mediation helps

Mediation works well when the parties will keep dealing with one another, when the facts are largely agreed, and when speed and privacy matter. A neutral person helps each side understand the other and test its position.

## When a court is the right place

A court can order something a settlement cannot, such as a ruling on a legal question or enforcement against a party who will not engage. We will tell you honestly which route fits your situation and what each is likely to cost.

title: When an employee leaves: a short checklist for owners
author: daniel-vance
summary: Final pay, equipment, access and paperwork: what to do on the last day.
body:
A departure goes better when the steps are decided in advance.

## The checklist

Pay the final wages on time and in the way the law and your policy require. Collect equipment and remove access to systems and accounts. Provide required notices about benefits. Remind the employee of any confidentiality agreement they signed. Keep a short, factual record of what was done and when.

## Tone matters

Most disputes after a departure grow from how the person was treated at the end. A brief, respectful conversation is worth more than any form.
